title: Bobby
full_review:
A conventional biography of presidential candidate Robert F. Kennedy, whose life ended abruptly with an assassin's bullet in 1968, "Bobby" (MGM/Weinstein) is not.

But director-writer Emilio Estevez has instead fashioned a deft intertwining of fact and fiction that pays touching homage to a fallen hero. Using multiple stories and disparate characters whose lives will eventually intertwine and find redemption, Estevez focuses on the fictitious guests and workers at the Ambassador Hotel in Los Angeles, leading up to Kennedy's brutal shooting in the hotel's kitchen after he delivered a rousing campaign speech following the California primary.

The players include the hotel's retired doorman, John Casey (Anthony Hopkins), who fondly remembers the hotel's golden days with fabled Hollywood stars; another retiree, Nelson (Harry Belafonte), John's chess partner; idealistic kitchen worker Jose (Freddy Rodriguez); sous chef Edward (Laurence Fishburne), with whom Jose bonds; bigoted kitchen manager Timmons (Christian Slater); alcoholic singer Virginia Fallon (Demi Moore) and her estranged husband, Tim (Estevez himself); a bride-to-be, Diane (Lindsay Lohan), marrying William Avery (Elijah Wood) to save him from Vietnam; a drug dealer (Ashton Kutcher) who gives two of RFK's young campaign workers (Brian Geraghty and Shia Lebeouf) their first LSD; a troubled East Coast couple (Estevez's dad, Martin Sheen, and Helen Hunt); the hotel manager, Paul (William H. Macy), and his hairdresser wife, Miriam (Sharon Stone), and so on.

Kennedy is only seen sporadically in newsreel footage (well-restored for the big screen) but Estevez's characters -- despite conflicts -- ultimately come to reflect the noble ideals of brotherhood and forgiveness expressed in some of Kennedy's stirring campaign speeches.

Miriam, for instance, discovers her husband's affair with switchboard operator Angela (Heather Graham), but the ultimate confrontation is not the expected screaming match, but a speech of profound regret tinged with caring. At another point, the scene is set for a no-holds-barred confrontation between Miriam and Virginia, but the conversation is instead suffused with empathy.

Though this approach sometimes results in oversentimentality as when Jose selflessly hands over his Dodgers tickets to Edward without asking for payment, prompting the latter to praise him effusively for his kingly nature (with reference to John F. Kennedy's favorite book, "The Once and Future King"), such missteps are few.

The film also demonstrates an admirable respect for marriage, when Diane suggests to William that, draft issues aside, perhaps they might really make it work. And there are many other such reconciliatory moments, where prejudice, class differences and even just pointless misunderstandings are dispelled.

The assassination sequence, by the way, is a skillful mixing of archival footage and re-creation. No matter your political stripe, "Bobby" is compelling drama and demonstrates a rare humanity.

This film contains some rough expletives and an instance of profanity, drug use, brief side and rear nudity, brief violence and an adulterous affair. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted. Under 17 requires accompanying parent or adult guardian.
